unit.title: Coordinate and manage basic installation projects

summary: This unit teaches you to run a small electrical installation job from start to finish: agreeing the scope, building a programme with milestones, organising people, tools and materials, fitting in with the other trades, keeping the site safe, controlling changes, cost and progress, and handing the finished work over to the client. You will also learn the simple sums a coordinator uses every week and how to review a job so the next one goes better.

blocks.p: At Level 3 you are no longer only the person who wires. On a small job, such as a shop, a house, a small office or a church hall, you may be the **coordinator**: the person who brings the people, materials, information and work together so the job is done safely, on time, to the drawings and within the budget. You still need to know the wiring, because you check it, but your main tools are the plan, the programme, the site diary and clear communication.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Have the signed scope, price, specification and latest drawings in hand; walk the site; set up the store, first aid, fire extinguisher, signs and waste area; hold a start-up meeting.
Break the job into stages, estimate the labour hours, set milestones, link them to the builder's programme, and allow time for the government inspection and the JPS connection.
Plan the team, tools, plant and materials for each stage; order long-lead items early; share equipment between jobs without clashes.
Give each person a clear task with a job card, put competent people on critical work, brief the team daily and balance the workload.
Fit the electrical work around the masons, plumber, carpenter, A/C installer and painter; manage subcontractors; deal with the client, the inspector and JPS.
Make sure risk assessments, method statements, toolbox talks, permits, PPE, barriers and safe isolation are in place and used; deal with near misses and emergencies.
Handle variations in writing; track hours, materials and money against the plan; spot and deal with delays early.
Inspect at each stage before work is covered, correct faults, and find out why they happened.
Clear the snag list, have the work tested and passed, hand over the documents and show the client how to use the installation safely.
Collect the facts, hold a review meeting and use the lessons on the next job.

blocks.h: Who does what on a small project

head: Person or body
Their part
rows: Pays for the work, agrees the scope and approves changes. Names one contact person if possible.
Produces the drawings and specification and issues revisions.
Runs the whole building job and its programme; the electrical firm often works under the builder.
Plans and runs the electrical work, leads the team and is the link to everyone else.
Do the work to the drawings and job cards, safely, and report problems.
Firms hired to do part of the work, such as trenching or a fire alarm.
Provide materials and equipment to agreed dates.
Licensed electrical inspector, under the Government Electrical Regulator (GER)
Inspects and certifies the installation before JPS will connect it.
Provides the service and the meter, and energises the supply once the installation is certified.

blocks.p: Everyone who is involved in, or affected by, the project is a **stakeholder**: the client and their staff, neighbours, the other trades, suppliers, the inspector and JPS. A good coordinator thinks about all of them, not only the person paying.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, a new or altered installation must be inspected and certified by a licensed electrical inspector, under the **Government Electrical Regulator (GER)**, before JPS will connect the supply. JPS also needs an application and paperwork for a new service. Both take time, so both belong in your programme from the start.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Most problems on a project start before the first cable is pulled: an unclear scope, an old drawing, materials ordered late, or nobody knowing who gives instructions. The first week sets the tone for the whole job.

blocks.h: Documents you need before work starts

head: Document
Why you need it
rows: Signed **scope** of work, with a list of what is **not** included (exclusions)
Both sides know exactly what the price covers. Exclusions, such as builder's work in chasing walls or supplying the A/C units, stop arguments later.
Sets what the client will pay and how payments are staged.
Show what to install and where. Working from an old revision means doing work twice.
Sets the materials, workmanship and tests required.
Shows when the building will be ready for each electrical stage.
Show how each main task will be done safely; the team must read them.

blocks.p: Drawings change during a job. Each new issue has a **revision letter or number** (A, B, C…) and a date. When revision C arrives, issue it to everyone who needs it and **remove or clearly mark old copies as superseded**, so nobody works from revision B. Keep a simple register of drawings: number, title, current revision, date received and who has copies.

blocks.h: The first week, step by step

flow: Check the scope, price, specification and drawings are agreed, signed and current
Walk the site with the builder: access, storage, power for tools, hazards and the neighbours
Draft the programme and milestones, linked to the builder's programme
Plan the team and materials; order long-lead items such as the main board
Set up the site: lockable store, first-aid kit, fire extinguisher, signs and a waste area
Hold the start-up meeting: contacts, who gives instructions, how changes are approved
Open the site diary; brief the team with the risk assessment, toolbox talk and job cards

ul: A **lockable store** or container for tools and materials, out of the rain.
A **first-aid kit**, a trained first-aider and the address of the nearest hospital or health centre.
A **fire extinguisher** suitable for electrical fires (CO2 or dry powder) where the team works.
Warning signs and barriers ready for work areas, open trenches and boards with covers off.
A place for waste: cable offcuts, drums, packaging and broken blocks. Planning how waste leaves site is the **coordinator's** job, not something left for the next trade.
Welfare: drinking water, shade, toilets and a place to eat. Jamaican heat makes water and shade a safety matter, not a comfort.

blocks.p: Hold a short meeting with the client, the builder and the other trades before work starts. Agree: one contact person on each side; how and when progress will be reported; who may give instructions to the electrical team (only you, after agreeing with the client); how changes are requested, priced and approved; working hours and access; and the key dates. Write **minutes**: who attended, what was decided and who will act, by when. Send them to everyone.

blocks.note: If the scope is not signed, or the drawings are not at their latest revision, do not let work start 'to save time'. Work done to the wrong information usually has to be done twice.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The **programme** (schedule) is the timed list of all the project's tasks with their start and finish dates. On a small job it is usually drawn as a **bar chart (Gantt chart)**: tasks down the side, dates across the top, and a bar for each task.

flow: List the stages: set-up, first fix (containment, boxes, cables in walls and roof), board and sub-mains, second fix (accessories and fittings), testing, inspection, JPS connection, handover
Estimate the labour hours for each stage from the drawings and past jobs
Decide the team size and work out each stage's duration
Put the stages in order and link them to the builder's programme
Mark the milestones
Check the critical path and the long-lead items
Share the programme and update it every week

blocks.p: A **milestone** is a key event with a date, not a task with a length: 'first fix complete and inspected', 'board energised for testing', 'inspection passed', 'JPS connection', 'handover'. Milestones let everyone see quickly whether the job is on track, and they are often linked to stage payments.

Some tasks must follow each other: you cannot do second fix before plastering, or have the inspection before testing. The longest chain of linked tasks through the job is the **critical path**. It sets the shortest possible time for the whole job. A delay to any task on the critical path delays the finish date. A task off the critical path has some **float** (spare time) and can slip a little without moving the finish.

head: Example task
Depends on
On the critical path?
rows: Conduit and boxes in block walls
Yes, if it arrives later than the board is needed
Yes: JPS will not connect before it is passed

blocks.p: Labour is planned in **person-hours** (also called man-hours): one person working one hour. Duration depends on how many people share the work.

head: Sum
Method
Example
rows: Count working days only (usually Monday to Friday), skipping public holidays
Start Tuesday 3 June, 7 working days: finishes Wednesday 11 June

blocks.note: When counting working days, count the start day as day 1. Check the calendar for Jamaican public holidays, such as Labour Day (23 May), Emancipation Day (1 August) and Independence Day (6 August): no work, or overtime rates, on those days.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **long-lead item** is anything that takes a long time to arrive: a main switchboard, a generator, an automatic transfer switch, special light fittings. Order them as soon as the design is agreed. Also build in time for things you do not control: the government inspection and any re-inspection, and the JPS application and connection. JPS may need weeks to provide a new service, especially if its line or transformer needs work, so start the paperwork early.

blocks.h: Planning for risk in the programme

ul: **Weather**: rain in the rainy seasons (roughly May–June and September–November) delays trenching, roof work and outdoor work. Plan indoor tasks that can go ahead on wet days.
**Hurricane season** (June to November): plan to secure the site, materials and equipment when a storm is forecast.
**Late deliveries**: allow some float before work that depends on long-lead items.
**Other trades running late**: watch the builder's programme each week.
**Shutdowns** in occupied buildings: agree them with the client well ahead.

sections.title: Resources, people and the other trades

head: Resource
What to plan
rows: How many electricians, trainees and helpers each stage needs, and when; who is competent for critical tasks such as terminating the board and testing.
A take-off from the drawings, with order dates so materials arrive when needed, not weeks early (theft, damage) or late (idle team).
Drills, benders, cable-pulling winch, access towers, scaffold, test instruments with calibration in date.
Current drawings, specification and makers' instructions on site.
The budget for each stage, and a **contingency**: a sum set aside for unexpected costs.

blocks.p: When two jobs need the same item, such as the firm's only winch or insulation tester, on the same day, deal with it in advance: move one job's task to another day, or hire a second item. Do not leave it to whichever team reaches the store first, and never let a team improvise unsafely without the right equipment.

ul: Put **competent** people on critical and safety work: terminating and testing a board is for a qualified electrician, with a trainee helping and learning.
Give trainees tasks that suit their level, with supervision.
Balance the workload. If one electrician has three tasks for one morning and another has none, share them out.
Give each person a **job card**: the task, the place, the drawing, the materials, the hazards and controls, and the time allowed. It saves questions and mistakes, and shows what has been done.

head: Meeting
When
Purpose
rows: The day's tasks and the day's hazards, such as work at height or a shutdown.
Progress against the programme, problems, who will act and by when. Minutes are kept.
At the start and end of the job
Agree the rules; hand over the finished work.

blocks.h: Fitting in with the other trades

blocks.p: On a new building the electrical work comes in stages between the other trades. The usual order on a Jamaican block-and-concrete house is:

flow: Slab and foundation: conduit or sleeves for the service and any floor outlets cast in
Block walls: conduit and boxes built in as the masons go up, or chased in before plastering
Roof and ceilings: first fix in the roof before the carpenter closes the ceilings
Stage inspection of first fix, before it is covered
Plastering and the painter's first coat
Second fix: switches, outlets, fittings and the board after plastering and first coat
Testing, inspection, JPS connection

head: Trade
What to agree with them
rows: When conduit and boxes go into walls and columns, and that nothing is plastered over before it is checked.
Routes through walls and ceilings, keeping cables clear of hot pipes and water; who goes first in shared spaces.
Positions of cable drops and fittings before ceilings close; access hatches.
The position of the 220 V supply point and isolator for each unit, agreed at planning and marked on the drawing.
Second fix after the first coat, so accessories are not painted over; protecting finished work.

blocks.note: When two trades want the same space on the same day, agree routes and times **beforehand**, with the builder if needed. 'Sorting it out on the day' means one team stands idle or work is done in the wrong order.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **subcontractor** is a firm hired to do part of the work, such as digging a cable trench. You remain responsible for the result. Before they start, check that they are competent, that they have the drawing and the specification, and that buried services have been found (drawings, a cable locator, asking JPS, the water company and the client). Inspect their work before you build on it: a trench that is shallower than the drawing must be corrected **before** the cable is laid, not accepted to save time.
As coordinator you plan safety into the job and check that it happens. The team must never be put in a position where the programme pushes them to cut corners.

blocks.h: The safety system for a small site

head: Item
What it is
Your job
rows: A written list of the hazards of each task, who could be harmed and the controls.
Make sure one exists for each main task and that the team has read it.
The steps of a task in order, with the safety controls at each step.
Use it to brief the team; update it when the method changes.
A first-day talk for everyone new to site: hazards, rules, first aid, fire, emergency plan.
Give it, and record who has had it.
A short talk on site about the day's hazards.
Hold one at the start of each day or task.
A written approval that sets the safe conditions, the time and the people for a high-risk task, such as work on a factory roof or in a plant room.
Get it from the client's authorised person before starting, and work only within it. It never allows live work.
Boots, glasses, hard hats, gloves; ladders, steps and towers.
Check they are provided, in good order and used.

blocks.h: Protecting the client's staff and the public

blocks.p: In an occupied building, people will walk into your work area unless you stop them. Put up **barriers and signs**, keep covers on boards when nobody is working on them, and agree access routes with the client, for example a side door while floor boxes are fitted in the main corridor. Keep walkways clear of cables, offcuts and tools: housekeeping is checked every day.

Every circuit is worked on dead. The procedure is the same on every job: identify the circuit; switch off; **lock off** with each worker's own padlock (a multi-lock hasp if several people work on it); **tag**; prove the voltage tester on a proving unit; **prove dead** at the point of work between all conductors; prove the tester again. Locks come off only when each worker is finished and clear, and only the authorised person restores the supply.

blocks.note: Never plan 'live work if we run late'. If a shutdown is running over time, tell the client and agree what to do. Pressure on time is the commonest reason people take risks with live conductors.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: A **near miss** is an event that could have caused injury or damage but did not, such as a ladder slipping on a tiled floor. Record it, find the cause and fix it before work goes on (for example, use ladder feet suitable for tiles, or a tower). Telling the worker to be careful does not remove the cause.

If someone gets an electric shock: **switch off the supply first** (or move them clear with something dry and non-conducting), then give first aid and call **110** for an ambulance. Never touch a casualty who may still be in contact with the supply.
Report every accident and near miss on the firm's form, with facts, and keep a copy in the project file.
If another trade damages a cable, isolate it, make it safe, barrier it and record it in the diary; then agree the repair.

blocks.p: Connecting new circuits in a working office, shop or school usually means switching off part of the existing installation. A shutdown affects the client's business, so it is planned like a small project of its own.

flow: Find exactly which boards and circuits will be off, from the drawings and a survey
Agree the date, start time and length with the client, often a weekend or evening
The client warns staff, saves computer work, and protects servers, fridges and alarms
Prepare everything beforehand: new circuits run, terminated and tested dead up to the point of connection
On the day, brief the team on the method and hazards
Safe isolation: off, lock, tag, prove dead with a tester checked before and after
Make the connections; inspect and test them dead
Remove locks only when everyone is clear; the authorised person restores the supply
Check with the client that everything is working, and record the shutdown in the diary

blocks.note: Doing as much as possible **before** the shutdown keeps the power-off time short. A shutdown that overruns because materials were not ready is the coordinator's failure, not the team's.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Watch for other sources of supply: a standby generator with an automatic transfer switch can start when you switch off the main, and solar PV inverters or UPS units can keep circuits live. Isolate and lock off every source.

ul: Agree one contact person each way.
Give short, factual progress reports: 'Ground floor first fix complete; first floor 50%, due Thursday; board delivered.' Not 'going well'.
Confirm every instruction given by phone or on site **in writing** (email or message) and keep a copy.
Warn early about delays, shutdowns or extra costs, with the reason and what you will do.
Only you give the team instructions about changes, after agreeing them with the client. Instructions from anyone else in the client's office go through you.

head: Record
What goes in it
rows: Date and weather; who was on site; work done; visitors; deliveries; delays and their causes; instructions received; accidents and near misses.
Who attended, what was decided, who will act and by when.
Each drawing's number, current revision and who has copies.
Hours worked by each person on each stage, checked weekly against the plan.
Each change, its price and time, and the client's written approval.
Stage checks, snag lists and test results.

blocks.p: Records protect everyone. When there is an argument about why the job finished late or what the client asked for, the diary and the written confirmations settle it.
A **variation** (variation order, change order) is a change to the agreed work that alters the price or the time, such as six extra outlets or a new outside light. Handle every one the same way:

flow: Write down exactly what the client wants
Check the effect on the design: load, cable sizes, board ways, drawings
Price the extra materials and labour, and the effect on the programme
Send a written variation with the cost and new finish date
Wait for written approval
Update the drawings, order materials, change the programme, brief the team
Inspect and test the extra work, mark it on the as-built drawings, add it to the final account

blocks.note: Fitting extra work 'to keep the client happy' and adding it to the bill later is how disputes start. Refusing outright is not right either. Price it, get it approved in writing, then do it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Each week compare what has been done, and what it has cost, with the plan. The earlier you see a problem, the cheaper it is to fix.

Compare the **percentage of work complete** with the **percentage of hours (or money) used**. If first fix is 50% complete but 70% of its hours are gone, the stage is running over: at that rate it will need about 140% of its planned hours. If the work done is ahead of the hours used, the stage is doing better than planned.

head: Question
Method
Example
rows: By what percentage is a cost over budget?
What is the week's labour cost?
By what percentage is the job late?
% hours used compared with % work done
40% done, 40% of hours used: on track

blocks.note: Always say what a percentage is a percentage **of**. An overrun is measured against the plan or budget, not against the actual figure.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Find the cause: late materials, too few people, rework, waiting for another trade, weather
Decide the action: change the order of tasks, add a person, agree extra hours, chase the supplier
Tell your manager and the client early, with the reason and a new forecast date
Update the programme and keep safety and quality checks in place

blocks.p: Example: the light fittings will arrive a week late. Do not stop the whole job and do not buy any fittings from the nearest shop. Re-plan so other tasks go ahead (outlets, board, testing of other circuits), confirm the new delivery date in writing, and check whether the delay touches the critical path or the inspection date.

ul: Plan **internal inspections at stages**: after first fix and before walls and ceilings close, after board installation, before the government inspection. Faults found early are cheap to fix; faults found behind plaster are not.
Check against the drawings and specification: positions and heights, cable sizes, colours, fixings, labels.

When you find a fault, such as switches fixed at 1.0 m where the drawing says 1.2 m, have it **corrected** and find out **why** it happened (wrong drawing revision? unclear job card? no setting-out?), so it does not happen again.
Never change a drawing to match faulty work, and never hope the inspector will not notice.

blocks.h: Preparing for the government inspection and JPS

flow: Find out early what the inspector and JPS need; start the JPS service application
Carry out your own stage inspections during the job
Near the end: full own inspection and dead tests; fix every defect; record the results
Board labelled, circuit chart filled in, covers fitted, earthing and bonding complete
Book the inspection, with a competent electrician present to answer questions
Correct any defects and arrange a re-inspection if needed
Once certified, arrange the JPS connection and who will be present

blocks.p: A **snag list** (punch list) is a list of the small items still to finish or correct before handover: a missing blanking plate, a crooked switch, a label not fixed, paint on an outlet. Walk the job with the team, write the list with locations, give each item an owner and a date, and tick it off. Hand over only when it is cleared, or agree the remaining items with the client in writing.

head: Show the client
Give the client
rows: Where the main switch is and how to isolate in an emergency
How to reset a breaker, and when not to
How to test the GFCI outlets with the TEST button
Any special equipment: generator changeover, timers, sensors
Test results and the inspection certificate
**As-built drawings**: the installation as finally built, with every change
An up-to-date circuit chart in the board
Your contact details and the warranty period

blocks.p: Ask the client to sign that they have received the work and the documents. Leave the site clean. **Unused materials** are counted, recorded and returned to the store, or to the client if they paid for them; they are not thrown away or taken home.

Soon after handover, gather the facts: planned and actual hours and costs for each stage, defects found at inspection, accidents and near misses, delays and their causes, and the client's feedback. Hold a short review with the team. The aim is to **learn**, not to blame.

ul: What went well, and why? Keep doing it.
What went badly, and why? For example, a re-inspection was needed because labels were missing.
What will we do differently? For example, add labelling to the pre-inspection checklist; order fittings two weeks earlier.
Update the firm's estimating figures with the real hours, so the next price is more accurate.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can list the documents a coordinator needs before work starts, and explain why exclusions matter.
I can set up a small site and run a start-up meeting.
I can control drawing revisions so nobody works from an old copy.
I can build a programme with stages, milestones and links to the builder's programme.
I can explain the critical path and float, and name long-lead items.
I can work out person-hours, durations, finish dates, costs and percentages.
I can plan people, tools and materials, and settle a clash over shared equipment.
I can give job cards and balance the team's workload.
I can fit the electrical stages around the masons, plumber, carpenter, A/C installer and painter.
I can check a subcontractor's work before building on it.
I can put the site safety system in place, including permits, barriers and safe isolation.
I can plan a shutdown in an occupied building.
I can handle a variation from request to final account.
I can keep a site diary, minutes and written confirmations.
I can spot a stage that is running over and decide what to do.
I can plan stage inspections and deal with a quality fault.
I can prepare for the inspection and the JPS connection.
I can clear a snag list and hand over with the right documents.
I can review a finished project and use the lessons.

terms: As-built drawings
Drawings showing the installation as it was finally built, with every change; also called record drawings.
Bar chart (Gantt chart)
A programme drawn as bars against dates, one bar per task.
Contingency
A sum kept in the budget for unexpected costs.
Critical path
The longest chain of linked tasks; it sets the shortest possible time for the job.
Exclusions
Work that is not included in the price, listed with the scope.
First fix / second fix
First fix: containment, boxes and cables before plastering and ceilings. Second fix: accessories and fittings after plastering and painting.
Float
Spare time a task can slip without delaying the finish date.
Job card
A written instruction for one task: what, where, materials, hazards and time allowed.
Long-lead item
Equipment that takes a long time to deliver and must be ordered early.
Milestone
A key event with a date, such as 'first fix complete'.
Minutes
The written record of a meeting: who attended, what was decided and who will act.
Near miss
An event that could have caused injury or damage but did not.
Permit to work
A written approval setting the safe conditions for a high-risk task.
Person-hour
One person working for one hour; the unit for planning labour.
Programme
The timed list of a project's tasks with start and finish dates.
Scope
The agreed description of the work the price covers.
Site diary
The daily record of work, people, visitors, delays and instructions.
Snag list (punch list)
Small items to finish or correct before handover.
Stakeholder
Anyone involved in or affected by the project.
Subcontractor
A firm hired by the contractor to do part of the work.
Toolbox talk
A short talk on site about the day's hazards.
Variation
A change to the agreed work that alters the price or time; also called a change order.

c1.title: A pharmacy fit-out in Santa Cruz
c1.text: Kemar, a Level 3 trainee, is coordinating the electrical fit-out of a new pharmacy in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, under his supervisor Mr Lloyd Brown. The builder's programme shows the block walls finished in week 2, plastering in week 4 and painting in week 6. The main board has a 5-week delivery from the supplier in Kingston. The scope is signed, but the architect has just emailed revision B of the floor plan, moving the dispensary counter and its outlets. The pharmacy owner, Mrs Forbes, wants to open in week 9.

c2.title: Rewiring a primary school in Black River
c2.text: A team of three electricians and two trainees is rewiring two classroom blocks at a primary school in Black River during the summer holidays. The job was planned at 480 person-hours over 12 working days. At the end of day 6 the site diary shows 280 hours used and the work about 45% complete. The school's office block, which is not part of the job, stays open, and the office staff must keep their computers running. One trainee reports that a stepladder slid on the polished corridor floor; nobody was hurt.

c3.title: A warehouse extension in Freeport, Montego Bay
c3.text: Ms Grant coordinates the electrical work for a warehouse extension at Freeport, Montego Bay. A subcontractor is digging the trench for the underground supply cable to the new building, and the client has asked for a 'permit to work' before anyone goes onto the roof to fit the floodlights. On Thursday the client's operations manager phones Ms Grant and asks for four extra 220 V outlets for charging forklifts, 'as soon as possible'. The materials budget is J$1 200 000 and J$1 290 000 has been committed so far.

c4.title: Handing over a guest house in Port Antonio
c4.text: The electrical installation of a six-room guest house in Port Antonio is finished. The team's own tests passed, the licensed inspector has certified the installation and JPS has connected the supply. The owner, Mr Chin, is due to take over on Friday. Walking round on Wednesday, the coordinator finds two missing blanking plates, a GFCI outlet in the kitchen that does not trip on TEST, and 60 m of unused cable and twelve light fittings in the store. The circuit chart in the board is blank.

c5.title: A church hall in Mandeville, reviewed
c5.text: A church hall in Mandeville was wired by a team of two electricians and a helper. The job was planned for 20 working days and took 25. Labour was planned at 400 person-hours and used 470. The inspector asked for a re-inspection because the board had no circuit chart and two circuits were unlabelled. The client, Pastor Reid, was happy with the finished work but said he was 'never sure what was happening week to week'.

questions.q: Revision B of the floor plan arrives by email. What should Kemar do with it first?
o: File it in the office and carry on with the plan already on site
Issue it to the team and mark every copy of revision A as superseded
Keep both revisions on site so the team can choose the clearer one
Wait until the architect visits the site to explain the changes
questions.why: Work must be done to the latest revision. Issuing revision B and removing or marking the old copies stops someone fixing the dispensary outlets in the old position. Keep the drawing register up to date, and ask the architect if anything on it is unclear.

questions.q: The walls are finished in week 2 and plastering starts in week 4. When must the conduit and boxes in the block walls be in and checked?
o: Before plastering starts in week 4
After plastering, so the plaster is not damaged
After the painter's first coat in week 6
In week 9, just before the opening
questions.why: Conduit and boxes in block walls are first-fix work and must be in place, and inspected, before the masons plaster over them. After plastering they can only be chased in, which damages the finish and costs time.

questions.q: Mrs Forbes wants to open in week 9, and the board takes 5 weeks to deliver. Which planning decision matters most for that date?
o: Ordering the board now, so it arrives in time for second fix and testing
Asking the supplier to deliver the board on the last day of the job
Leaving the board order until the plastering is finished
Ordering the board after the government inspection is booked
questions.why: The board is a long-lead item on the critical path: testing, inspection and the JPS connection all wait for it. Ordered now it arrives in week 5 or 6, in time for second fix; ordered later it pushes the opening past week 9.

questions.q: Kemar lists the dates by which the pharmacy must be inspected and connected. What is the correct order of these two steps?
o: JPS connects the supply, then the licensed inspector certifies the work
The licensed inspector certifies the installation, then JPS connects it
Both happen on the same visit, arranged by the pharmacy owner
The inspection is only needed if JPS asks for it after connection
questions.why: In Jamaica the installation must be inspected and certified by a licensed inspector, under the Government Electrical Regulator, before JPS will energise the supply. The programme needs time for both, and for any re-inspection.

questions.q: After day 6 the school job has used 280 of 480 planned hours and is about 45% complete. What does this show?
o: The job is ahead of plan and will finish under its labour budget
The job is exactly on track with the plan and needs no action
The job is behind: over half the hours are gone for under half the work
The hours were planned too high, so the figures mean nothing yet
questions.why: 280 ÷ 480 is about 58% of the hours used for 45% of the work. At that rate the stage will need well over its planned hours. Find the cause now and act, rather than waiting for the end.

questions.q: If the team keeps working 8-hour days, how many person-hours does the school team of five use in one day?
o: 24 person-hours
40 person-hours
48 person-hours
13 person-hours
questions.why: Person-hours = people × hours: 5 × 8 = 40. Trainees count as people on the timesheet even though they work under supervision.

questions.q: The new classroom circuits must be connected at a board that also feeds the office block. How should the coordinator arrange this?
o: Switch off the board at midday, when the office staff are all out at lunch
Agree a shutdown time with the school so the office can save work and switch off
Connect the new circuits live, since the office block cannot be interrupted
Ask the office staff to unplug their computers whenever a breaker trips
questions.why: A shutdown in an occupied building is agreed with the client in advance so they can protect staff, computers and data. The work is prepared beforehand to keep the power-off time short, and the circuits are safely isolated: never live.

questions.q: What is the right response to the stepladder that slid on the corridor floor?
o: Record it as a near miss, find why it slid and change the method first
Note it in the diary at the end of the job, since nobody was hurt by it
Remind the trainee to hold the ladder more firmly the next time he climbs
Move the stepladder to a classroom with a rougher floor and carry on
questions.why: A near miss is a free warning. Record it, find the cause (ladder feet, floor polish, no one footing it) and fix it, for example with a tower or suitable feet and a second person. Blaming the trainee leaves the hazard in place.

questions.q: The principal asks the coordinator who may tell the team to move an outlet position. What is the correct answer?
o: Any teacher who is in the classroom at the time
Only the coordinator, after agreeing the change with the school
The most senior electrician, whenever the school asks him
The trainee nearest to the principal when the request is made
questions.why: Instructions to the team come through one person, the coordinator, after the change has been agreed with the client and, where it changes cost or time, written up as a variation. Otherwise the team gets conflicting instructions and work is done twice.

questions.q: On the morning the trench is to be dug, the subcontractor's foreman says he has not seen the cable route drawing but 'knows where it goes'. What should Ms Grant do?
o: Let him start, since he has dug many trenches before this one
Give him the drawing and confirm route, depth and buried services first
Dig the trench with her own team instead and send him home
Tell him to dig where he thinks and move the cable later if needed
questions.why: The subcontractor must work from the current drawing: the route, the depth and the known buried services are on it. A few minutes of briefing avoids a wrong route, a shallow trench or a strike on a buried service.

questions.q: The client requires a permit to work before the roof floodlights are fitted. What does the permit do?
o: It allows the floodlights to be wired while the circuit is live
It records the price agreed for the roof work
It sets the safe conditions, time and people for the roof task
It lets the team use the client's canteen and car park
questions.why: A permit to work is a written approval from the client's authorised person that states the task, the precautions, who may do it and for how long. It controls a high-risk task; it never permits live work.

questions.q: The operations manager phones for four extra forklift-charging outlets. What should Ms Grant do before the team fits them?
o: Fit them at once and add the cost quietly to the final bill
Refuse them, because they are not shown on the current drawings
Write up the request, price the cost and time, and get written approval
Tell the team to fit them that day if there is spare cable in the van
questions.why: Extra 220 V outlets change the load, the board and the price: that is a variation. Record exactly what is wanted, check the design effect, send a written variation and start only after written approval. Then update the drawings and programme.

questions.q: Materials of J$1 290 000 have been committed against a budget of J$1 200 000. By what percentage is the materials budget overrun?
questions.why: Overrun = (actual − budget) ÷ budget × 100 = 90 000 ÷ 1 200 000 × 100 = 7.5%. The overrun is measured against the budget, not against the actual cost.

questions.q: Ms Grant notices that the subcontractor's trench is 400 mm deep where the drawing calls for 600 mm. What should she do?
o: Have it dug to 600 mm before the cable is laid
Lay the cable now and note the depth on the as-built drawing
Change the drawing to 400 mm to match the trench
Accept it, because the cable is armoured
questions.why: The depth on the drawing protects the cable from future digging and is part of the specification. The coordinator checks a subcontractor's work before building on it and has it corrected, which is far cheaper before the cable goes in than after.

questions.q: The kitchen GFCI outlet does not trip when its TEST button is pressed. What should go on the snag list?
o: Nothing, because the inspector has already passed the installation
Replace the GFCI outlet and test it again before handover
Tell Mr Chin to press the button harder each month
Change the outlet for an ordinary outlet so that it does not trip
questions.why: A GFCI that does not trip on test may not protect anyone from a shock, and the kitchen outlet needs that protection. It is a defect to correct and retest before handover, whatever was passed earlier.

questions.q: What should happen to the 60 m of cable and twelve light fittings left in the store?
o: Share them among the team as a bonus for finishing the job on time
Leave them in the guest house store for the next electrician who comes
Count and record them, then return them to the store or to Mr Chin
Put them in the skip with the packaging when the site is cleared
questions.why: Unused materials are recorded and returned to the firm's store, or handed to the client if they paid for them. A record protects the firm and the team from any suggestion that materials went missing.

questions.q: At the handover walk-round, which of these should the coordinator show Mr Chin?
o: How to replace a breaker with a larger one if it keeps tripping
How to find the main switch and isolate the supply in an emergency
How to remove the board cover to check the connections
How to bypass a GFCI outlet that trips when the kettle is used
questions.why: The client must be able to isolate the installation in an emergency, reset a breaker and test the GFCIs. Changing breaker sizes, opening the board and bypassing protection are dangerous and are never shown to a client.

questions.q: Which set of documents belongs in Mr Chin's handover pack?
o: The team's timesheets, the supplier invoices and the firm's pay records
The firm's price list, the van's insurance papers and the fuel receipts
The test results, inspection certificate, as-built drawings and manuals
The site diary, the risk assessments and the toolbox talk attendance register
questions.why: The client receives what they need to use, maintain and prove the installation: test results and the certificate, as-built drawings, a completed circuit chart, manuals and warranties. Timesheets, invoices and the diary stay in the firm's project file.

questions.q: By what percentage did the church hall job overrun its planned time?
questions.why: Overrun = days late ÷ planned days × 100 = 5 ÷ 20 × 100 = 25%. The 70 extra labour hours were a separate 17.5% overrun on hours.

questions.q: At the review meeting, which action best uses what the church hall job taught?
o: Find who forgot the circuit chart and warn them in front of the whole team
Add labelling to the pre-inspection checklist and start weekly written reports
Raise the firm's prices by 25% so that future overruns are covered in full
Decide that the inspector was unreasonable and carry on the same way
questions.why: A review looks for causes and fixes them: a checklist stops the re-inspection happening again, and a weekly report answers Pastor Reid's complaint. The real hours also go into the firm's estimating figures. Blame teaches nobody.
